en: Itivuttaka 44 Dukanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said. This discourse was spoken by the Blessed One while staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Having understood the meaning, the Venerable Ānanda spoke thus: “Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The person who is a speaker but not a doer, and the person who is both a speaker and a doer. These, monks, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is well said. Ānanda, it is well said. There are indeed these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The person who is a speaker but not a doer, and the person who is both a speaker and a doer. These, Ānanda, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The person who is a doer but not a speaker, and the person who is both a doer and a speaker. These, Ānanda, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The Discourse on the Element of Nibbāna.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
"Monks, there are these two elements of Nibbāna."
Which two?
The element of nibbāna with residue remaining and the element of nibbāna without residue remaining.
And what, monks, is the element of nibbāna with residue remaining?

In this case, monks, a monk is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge.
While his five faculties still remain— by which, because they are not yet exhausted, he experiences the pleasant and the unpleasant and feels pleasure and pain—
the destruction of his lust, hatred, and delusion occurs.
This, monks, is called the element of nibbāna with residue remaining.
And what, monks, is the element of nibbāna without residue remaining?

Here, monks, a monk is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through final knowledge.
“Bhikkhus, for one who does not delight in any feelings here and now, they will become cool.
This, bhikkhus, is called the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.
These, bhikkhus, are the two Nibbāna-elements.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
"These two have been proclaimed by the One with Vision:”
By one who is independent and poised in the element of Nibbāna—
there is indeed one element here pertaining to the present life,
wherein the craving for existence is exhausted, yet a residue remains.
But that which pertains to the future life is without residue;
therein all states of existence cease entirely.
Those who, having understood this, [attain] the unconditioned state—
With minds liberated through the destruction of the guide to existence,
having attained the essence of the Dhamma,
those Tādins delight in its cessation and have abandoned all states of becoming.
"This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The seventh.
